narration.text: This lesson covers where you may not park. The guide makes you responsible for parking only in designated areas, lists places where parking is never allowed, and gives a set of no-parking distances measured from signs, driveways, fire stations, safety zones, railroad crossings and hydrants. There are six distances in this lesson, so we will group them to make them easier to keep straight. To remember: your parking responsibility; places never to park; no-parking distances. A helpful hook for this lesson: thirty signs, five drives, fifteen hydrants.

You are responsible for parking only in designated areas so your vehicle is not a hazard, and colored curbs can signal parking limits. Never park in an intersection or on a crosswalk, a sidewalk or a bicycle lane. So before measuring any distance, check that the place itself is allowed. Intersections, crosswalks, sidewalks and bike lanes are never parking places. To remember: park only in designated areas; do not create a hazard; colored curbs signal limits. narration.text: This lesson covers how to park once you have found a legal place. The guide sets rules for which way the vehicle faces and how far from the curb it sits, lists more places where parking is banned, explains curb colors, and gives two safety habits: setting the parking brake and opening your door with the Dutch Reach. Each one is simple, and each one has a detail worth remembering. To remember: direction and curb distance; other banned places; curbs, brakes and doors. A helpful hook for this lesson: with traffic, within twelve inches.

lines.text: Face the same way as traffic.
No more than twelve inches from the curb.

narration.text: A parked vehicle must face the same way as traffic and sit no more than twelve inches from the curb. The twelve-inch limit is a maximum distance from the curb. So a car parked facing the wrong way breaks the rule even if it is close to the curb, and a car more than twelve inches out breaks it even if it faces the right way. To remember: face the same way as traffic; no more than twelve inches from the curb; twelve inches is a maximum. A helpful hook for this lesson: with traffic, within twelve inches. In short: A parked vehicle must face the same way as traffic and sit no more than twelve inches from the curb.

Parking is also banned beside an already parked vehicle, in a construction zone, on a bridge, overpass, tunnel or underpass, and on a freeway shoulder except in an emergency. So double parking is not allowed, and neither is stopping to park on bridges, in tunnels or along a freeway shoulder unless there is a real emergency. These places join the list from the previous lesson. To remember: beside an already parked vehicle; construction zones; bridges and tunnels; freeway shoulder except emergencies. A helpful hook for this lesson: with traffic, within twelve inches.

lines.text: Yellow or red: loading or restriction.

narration.text: A white painted curb allows only short stops, while a yellow or red curb marks a loading zone or another restriction. The twelve-inch limit is a maximum distance from the curb, and white curbs allow brief stops while yellow or red curbs mean loading or other limits. So the curb color tells you how long you may stay, or whether you may stay at all. To remember: white curb: short stops only; yellow or red: loading or restriction; read the curb before you park. A helpful hook for this lesson: with traffic, within twelve inches.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Some learners read the twelve-inch rule as a minimum gap you must leave. It is not. The twelve-inch limit is a maximum distance from the curb. So a vehicle parked six inches from the curb meets the rule, and one parked eighteen inches out does not. The vehicle must also face the same way as traffic. To remember: it is a maximum; closer than twelve inches is fine. A helpful hook for this lesson: with traffic, within twelve inches. In short: A parked vehicle must face the same way as traffic and sit no more than twelve inches from the curb.

lines.text: Set the parking brake every time.

narration.text: Set the parking brake every time you park, and especially on a hill. When you get out, use the Dutch Reach. That means checking your mirrors, then opening the door with the hand farthest from it, which turns your body so you see approaching cyclists. So both habits protect others: the brake keeps the car in place, and the Dutch Reach helps you spot a cyclist before you open the door. To remember: set the parking brake every time; especially on a hill; dutch Reach: far hand opens the door. A helpful hook for this lesson: with traffic, within twelve inches.

In short: A white painted curb allows only short stops, while a yellow or red curb marks a loading zone or another restriction.

A white curb allows only short stops, while yellow or red curbs mark loading zones or other restrictions. Set the parking brake every time you park, and open your door with the Dutch Reach. narration.text: This lesson covers leaving children or animals alone in a parked vehicle. The guide sets two age rules for children, one that depends on whether the motor is running and one that does not. It also sets a rule for animals based on conditions, and it explains what police may do when no one nearby can open the vehicle. The two child ages are easy to confuse, so we will set them side by side. To remember: two age rules for children; animals in vehicles; when police may step in. A helpful hook for this lesson: under sixteen, engine on; under twelve, never.

lines.text: Under twelve, motor off: still a crime.

narration.text: Leaving a child younger than sixteen alone in a parked vehicle with the motor running is a crime. Leaving a child younger than twelve alone in a parked vehicle is a crime even with the motor off. The under-sixteen rule covers a child left in a parked vehicle with the engine running, while the under-twelve rule covers a child left alone in any parked vehicle. To remember: under sixteen, motor running: crime; under twelve, motor off: still a crime; two separate rules. A helpful hook for this lesson: under sixteen, engine on; under twelve, never.

narration.text: Leaving an animal alone in a vehicle is a crime when heat, cold, poor ventilation or lack of water could injure or kill it. If nobody nearby can open the vehicle, police may remove a child or animal by any reasonable means, and the officer or agency is not liable for the damage. So the law protects both children and animals, and it allows officers to act when needed. To remember: animals: heat, cold, air, water; A crime if conditions could harm it; police may remove a child or animal. A helpful hook for this lesson: under sixteen, engine on; under twelve, never.

The under-sixteen rule covers a child left in a parked vehicle with the engine running, while the under-twelve rule covers a child left alone in any parked vehicle. So an engine-off car with a ten-year-old inside still breaks the law. To remember: under twelve: any parked vehicle; under sixteen: engine running. A helpful hook for this lesson: under sixteen, engine on; under twelve, never.

Leaving an animal alone when heat, cold, poor ventilation or lack of water could injure or kill it is a crime. If no one nearby can open the vehicle, police may remove a child or animal by any reasonable means without liability for the damage. narration.text: This lesson covers the steps for parking maneuvers. The guide describes how to enter and leave perpendicular or angled spaces and how to parallel park and pull out again. Each maneuver has an order of steps, and a few steps carry an exact check point, such as when your bumpers line up. Learning the order makes each maneuver smoother and safer for others around you. To remember: angled and perpendicular spaces; parallel parking; leaving each kind of space. A helpful hook for this lesson: bumpers align, back in, stop short.

lines.text: Steer to the middle; center in lines.

narration.text: To pull into a perpendicular or angled space, check traffic, signal, creep forward while steering to the middle of the space, center between the lines, then stop and secure the vehicle. To leave, back straight out while watching traffic until your bumper clears the next vehicle, then turn the wheel sharply the way you want to go. So entering is slow and centered, and leaving starts straight before you turn. To remember: check traffic, signal, creep forward; steer to the middle; center in lines; leave: back straight, then turn.

To parallel park, back slowly until your front bumper lines up with the rear bumper of the car you are parking behind, then turn the wheel sharply and back in. Stop before you touch the bumper of the vehicle behind you, then pull forward so you end up no more than twelve inches from the curb. Entering a parallel space starts by backing until bumpers line up, and it ends no more than twelve inches from the curb. To remember: back until bumpers line up; turn sharply and back in; stop before touching; pull forward. A helpful hook for this lesson: bumpers align, back in, stop short.

The guide says to stop before you touch the bumper of the vehicle behind you, then pull forward so you end up no more than twelve inches from the curb. So the finish of a parallel park is a controlled stop short of the car behind, followed by a small pull forward. To remember: stop before you touch it; then pull forward to the curb. A helpful hook for this lesson: bumpers align, back in, stop short.

lines.text: Move over once your door passes the car ahead.

narration.text: When leaving a parallel space, signal, steer forward slowly, and move into the nearest lane once your front door passes the rear bumper of the car ahead. So the exit has its own check point, just like the entry. Your front door passing the car ahead tells you there is room to move fully into the lane without striking the parked vehicle in front of you. To remember: signal first; steer forward slowly; move over once your door passes the car ahead. A helpful hook for this lesson: bumpers align, back in, stop short. In short: to enter an angled space, check traffic, signal, creep forward while steering to the middle, center between the lines, then stop and secure the vehicle.

A helpful hook for this lesson: bumpers align, back in, stop short. In short: to leave an angled space, back straight out while watching traffic until your bumper clears the next vehicle, then turn the wheel sharply.

Parallel park by backing until your front bumper lines up with the rear bumper of the car ahead, turning sharply, stopping before the car behind, and ending within twelve inches of the curb. Leave by signaling and moving over once your door passes the car ahead. To remember: angled: creep in, back straight out; parallel: bumpers align, back in, stop short; pull out once your door clears.

narration.text: This lesson covers which way to turn your wheels when you park on a hill. The guide gives four cases: uphill against a tall curb, uphill with a low or rounded curb, downhill with a curb, and a hill with no curb. In each case the goal is the same, keeping a rolling car out of traffic, but the wheel direction changes. Set the parking brake in every case, as the earlier lesson explained. To remember: uphill with a tall curb; uphill with a low curb; downhill and no curb. A helpful hook for this lesson: uphill tall curb away; downhill toward.

Facing uphill with a low or rounded curb, turning the wheel toward the curb may be safer, because the car would then roll away from the road. So uphill, the height of the curb changes the answer. To remember: tall curb: turn away from it; back of the tire rests on the curb; low curb: toward it may be safer. A helpful hook for this lesson: uphill tall curb away; downhill toward.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Many drivers think the wheels always turn toward the curb on a hill. Uphill against a tall curb, you turn the wheel away so the tire's back edge catches the curb. With a low or rounded uphill curb, turning toward it may be safer. Downhill, the wheel turns toward the curb. So the right answer depends on whether you face uphill or downhill and on the curb. To remember: uphill tall curb: away; low uphill curb: toward may be safer. A helpful hook for this lesson: uphill tall curb away; downhill toward.

On a hill with no curb, turn the wheels toward the road edge so the car rolls away from traffic. Downhill the wheel turns toward the curb so the front of the tire meets it, and with no curb the wheels turn toward the road edge, away from traffic. To remember: downhill: turn toward the curb; front of the tire touches it; no curb: toward the road edge. A helpful hook for this lesson: uphill tall curb away; downhill toward. In short: facing uphill against a tall curb, turn the wheel away from the curb so the back of the front tire rests against it.

lines.text: Uphill low curb: toward may be safer.

narration.text: Here are all four cases together. Uphill against a tall curb, turn away from the curb so the back of the front tire rests against it. Uphill with a low or rounded curb, turning toward the curb may be safer. Downhill, turn toward the curb so the front of the front tire touches it. With no curb, turn the wheels toward the road edge. Each case keeps a rolling car away from traffic. To remember: uphill tall curb: away; uphill low curb: toward may be safer; downhill: toward; no curb: road edge. A helpful hook for this lesson: uphill tall curb away; downhill toward.

lines.text: Which way do the wheels turn?

On a hill with no curb, turn the wheels toward the road edge so the car rolls away from traffic. With a curb, the direction would depend on whether you face uphill or downhill.
